coredata.dc:description: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is widely used for various industrial applications. However, owing to its extremely slow breakdown rate, PET accumulates as plastic trash, which negatively affects the environment and human health. Here, we report two novel PET hydrolases: PpPETase from Pseudomonas paralcaligenes MRCP1333, identified in human feces, and ScPETase from Streptomyces calvus DSM 41452. These two enzymes can decompose various PET materials, including semicrystalline PET powders (Cry-PET) and low-crystallinity PET films (gf-PET). By structure-guided engineering, two variants, PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G and ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K were obtained that decompose Cry-PET 3.1- and 1.9-fold faster than their wild-type enzymes, respectively. The co-expression of ScPETase and mono-(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate hydrolase from Ideonella sakaiensis (IsMHETase) resulted in 1.4-fold more degradation than the single enzyme system. This engineered strain degraded Cry-PET and gf-PET by more than 40% and 6%, respectively, after 30 d. The concentrations of terephthalic acid (TPA) in the Cry-PET and gf-PET degradation products were 37.7% and 25.6%, respectively. The discovery of these two novel PET hydrolases provides opportunities to create more powerful biocatalysts for PET biodegradation.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is widely used for various industrial applications. However, owing to its extremely slow breakdown rate, PET accumulates as plastic trash, which negatively affects the environment and human health. Here, we report two novel PET hydrolases: PpPETase from Pseudomonas paralcaligenes MRCP1333, identified in human feces, and ScPETase from Streptomyces calvus DSM 41452. These two enzymes can decompose various PET materials, including semicrystalline PET powders (Cry-PET) and low-crystallinity PET films (gf-PET). By structure-guided engineering, two variants, PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G and ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K were obtained that decompose Cry-PET 3.1- and 1.9-fold faster than their wild-type enzymes, respectively. The co-expression of ScPETase and mono-(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate hydrolase from Ideonella sakaiensis (IsMHETase) resulted in 1.4-fold more degradation than the single enzyme system. This engineered strain degraded Cry-PET and gf-PET by more than 40% and 6%, respectively, after 30 d. The concentrations of terephthalic acid (TPA) in the Cry-PET and gf-PET degradation products were 37.7% and 25.6%, respectively. The discovery of these two novel PET hydrolases provides opportunities to create more powerful biocatalysts for PET biodegradation.

Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), one of the most widely used plastics, decomposes extremely slowly in the natural environment, thus polluting the environment. We discovered and expressed two new PET hydrolases and constructed a two-step hydrolase co-expression system, and the results showed that they had a good hydrolysis effect on PET plastic.

ce:section.ce:para: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a common synthetic plastic produced by the polymerization of ethylene glycol (EG) and TPA [1]. PET contributes considerably to environmental contamination because PET has its extremely slow degradation rate in the natural environment [2,3]. In recent decades, there has been growing concern regarding the detrimental effects of plastics on various ecosystems, including aquatic, terrestrial, and marine environments. Plastics can persist in the environment for hundreds of years, imposing appreciable strain on both the environment and human health [4–6]. Microplastics, plastic particles with sizes < 5 mm in diameter, are a major source of pollution [7]. Microplastics are abundant in agricultural soils, where they can accumulate in crops and spread throughout various parts of the plant, including the roots, leaves, and stems. The presence of microplastics has the potential to affect crop growth, alter the composition of soil microbial communities, and disrupt metabolic functions as soil ages. Consequently, the effects of microplastics can have broad implications for agroecosystems and terrestrial biodiversity [8]. Animals consume plastic and microplastic products, which have potentially lethal consequences [9]. Since the initial identification of microplastics in human fecal matter in 2019 [10], subsequent studies have revealed their presence in various organs, bodily fluids, and excretions associated with human digestive, respiratory, cardiovascular, and reproductive systems. These findings suggest that microplastics are widely distributed throughout the human body. Studies have shown that microplastics can affect the human digestive, respiratory, endocrine, reproductive, and immune systems to varying degrees [11].

The presence of microplastic pollution has led to the adaptation of environmental bacteria, enabling them to utilize plastic as a carbon source for growth and survival [12,13]. Over the past decade, considerable progress has been made in the enzymatic biodegradation of PET due to the discovery of several novel PET hydrolases from various bacteria [13–15]. A notable example is the discovery of I. sakaiensis, which produces the PET-degrading enzyme IsPETase, in 2016 [16]. IsPETase and IsMHETase have been shown to have considerable hydrolytic activity and specificity toward PET substrates [16–18]. Through examination of the crystal structure of IsPETase, the catalytic mechanism employed by PETases for PET degradation was elucidated by examining the crystal structure of IsPETase [18–20]. Currently, research is focused on enzyme engineering to enhance both the hydrolytic efficiency and thermal stability of IsPETase [21–26]. The mutant FAST-PETase, created using a machine learning algorithm, demonstrated the ability to effectively break down the vast majority of untreated post-consumer PET originating from 51 distinct thermoformed items in just one week [26,27]. However, despite the prevalence of PET in the environment, the known numbers and types of microbial strains and their associated PETases remain relatively limited. Hence, the discovery of additional PET-degrading enzymes is desirable to investigate the natural evolution of PET-degrading enzymes within the environment and advance the development of more efficient biocatalysts.

In addition to the discovery of novel PET-degrading microorganisms, metagenomic mining strategies are efficient means of identifying functional enzymes derived from intricate microecosystems [28,29]. Metagenomics is the process of obtaining potentially valid protein sequences and validating them by comparing them with homologous sequences obtained directly from environmental metagenomic libraries. This approach effectively avoids the need to isolate proteins from laboratory cultures of natural microorganisms and is a powerful tool for exploring the biology and molecular biodiversity of different natural environments. Recently, a leaf-branch compost cutinase (LCC), a thermophilic PETase, was identified using metagenomics [30]. LCC demonstrated significant PET depolymerization activity in a bioreactor operating at 72 °C, making it a promising candidate for biological recycling of PET [31,32]. Efforts are currently being made to discover novel PET-degrading enzymes, including those derived from various microorganisms and environmental metagenomes. Notable examples of PET-degrading enzymes include Thermobifida fusca cutinases (TfCut1 and 2) [33], Humicola insolens (HiC) [34], Thermobifida alba (Tha_Cut1) [35], Antarctic bacterium Moraxella sp. (Mors1) [36], PET2 [37], PET5 [37], PET6 [37], PET12 [37], Ple628 [38], Ple629 [38], PE-H [39], Cryptosporangium aurantiacum (CaPETase) [40], Rhizobacter gummiphilus (RgPETase) [41], and Burkholderiales bacterium (BbPETase) [42]. The discovery of these enzymes suggests that the prevalence of microbes with the ability to degrade PET is more extensive than initially anticipated. Therefore, it is imperative that additional PET enzymes be identified in a comprehensive metagenomic database, which contains several previously undocumented microbial origins.

In the present study, two PET hydrolases, PpPETase from P. paralcaligenes and ScPETase from S. calvus have been described. Both enzymes demonstrated a considerable ability to break down PET at room temperature. By employing structure-guided rational protein engineering techniques, two variants PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G and ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K, were successfully produced, which demonstrated significantly improved enzyme activity and thermostability, respectively, compared with wild-type enzymes. In addition, a co-expression system was developed for ScPETase and IsMHETase that capitalized on the secretory properties of ScPETase. This system successfully facilitated the degradation of the PET powder and film, resulting in the formation of TPA in a one-pot process.

Construction of a Co-expression System for ScPETase and IsMHETase
ce:section.ce:para: The DNA sequence of IsMHETase (NCBI Reference Sequence: WP_054022745.1) was synthesized by Beijing Tsingke Biotech Co., Ltd. (China). The IsMHETase gene was inserted into pET28a-ScPETase to form pET28a-ScPETase-IsMHETase. A ribosome-binding site (rbs, AAGGAGATATA) was inserted between the two genes to facilitate translation of the latter protein. The primers used are listed in Supplementary Table S4.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Recombinant protein expression and purification in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: The constructed vectors were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3), which was grown in lysogeny broth containing 100 mg/L kanamycin at 37 °C and 220 r.p.m. until the optical density of the culture broth reached a value of 0.6 at 600 nm. After induction with 0.5 mmol/L isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactoside (IPTG), the bacteria were grown for 24 h at 16 °C and 220 r.p.m. The cell pellets were collected by centrifugation at 4 °C and 5000 × g for 15 min. Cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (16 mmol/L Na2HPO4, 4 mmol/L NaH2PO4, 500 mmol/L NaCl, 10 mmol/L imidazole, 375 μL/L β-mercaptoethanol, pH 7.4) at 10% (w/v). The cells were disrupted by sonication. Cell debris and insoluble aggregates were removed by centrifugation (1 h, 4 °C, 5000 × g). The supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 µmol/L filter and added to Ni-NTA-packed columns equilibrated with lysis buffer. The column was washed with at least 10 column volumes (CV) of washing buffer (16 mmol/L Na2HPO4, 4 mmol/L NaH2PO4, 500 mmol/L NaCl, 50 mmol/L imidazole, 375 μL/L β-mercaptoethanol, pH 7.4) before elution with 3 CV of elution buffer (16 mmol/L Na2HPO4, 4 mmol/L NaH2PO4, 500 mmol/L NaCl, 250 mmol/L imidazole, 375 μL/L β-mercaptoethanol, pH 7.4). Eluted proteins were concentrated by centrifugal ultrafiltration and replaced with preservation buffer (16 mmol/L Na2HPO4, 4 mmol/L NaH2PO4, 500 mmol/L NaCl, 10 mmol/L dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane, 375 μL/L β-mercaptoethanol, pH 7.4) to remove imidazole. All protein purification experiments were performed at 4 °C. Purified proteins were verified using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. All reagents used in the experiments were purchased from Shanghai Titan Scientific Co., Ltd.(China).

The monomer bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) was purchased from Macklin Inc. (China, Cat. No.: H909109). The homogenous amorphous gf-PET film (Goodfellow, US 479–650-78; specification: density: 1.3–1.4 g cm−3, refractive index: 1.58–1.64, permeability to water: 100 × 10−13 cm3. cm cm−2 s−1 Pa−1 at 25 °C, coefficient of thermal expansion: 20–80 × 10−6 K−1, thermal conductivity: 0.13–0.15 W m−1 K−1 at 23 °C) and semi-crystalline PET powder (Cry-PET, Goodfellow, US 277–377-58; density: 1.3–1.4 g cm−3, specification: nominal granule size: 3–5 mm, refractive index: 1.58–1.64, coefficient of thermal expansion: 20–80 × 10−6 K−1, thermal conductivity: 0.15–0.40 W m−1 K−1 at 23 °C) were used as the substrate for degradation assays with the purified PETase enzyme and its variants. The gf-PET film was prepared in a circular form (6 mm in diameter, approximately 5 mg) and washed thrice with 1% SDS, 20% ethanol, and deionized water before use [41].

In a preliminary PET degradation assay of the 11 PETase candidates, the esterase activity of the purified enzymes was quantified using the substrate 4-nitrophenyl butyrate (pNPB, Macklin Inc., China, Cat. No. N832938). 5 µg enzyme and 10 μL of substrate solution (4 mmol/L pNPB in acetonitrile) were combined with 980 μL of 50 mmol/L phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.0) buffer at temperatures of 30 °C, 40 °C and 50 °C. Changes in absorbance were measured at 405 nm using a UV spectrophotometer. One unit (U) was defined as the amount of enzyme needed to release 1 µmol of pNPB per minute. 0.6 mmol/L BHET was soaked in 50 mmol/L PBS (pH 7.0) buffer with 2 µM enzyme. The reaction mixture (1 mL) was incubated at 30, 40, and 50 °C for 24 h. The reaction was terminated by the addition of a 1:1 solution of 2 mol/L sulfuric acid. The reaction mixtures were sampled at various time points to quantify the total amount of the released PET monomers. The reaction mixture was filtered using a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) syringe filter (0.22 µm) to eliminate the residual substrate and impurities. The samples were analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). All experiments were performed in triplicates. Data are presented as the mean values ± SDs.

The PET hydrolytic activity assay was performed using 0.6 mmol/L BHET, 15 mg of Cry-PET, and 15 mg of gf-PET film at 30 °C with 2 μmol/L enzymes in 1 mL of 50 mmol/L PBS (pH 7.0) buffer [40]. The reaction mixtures were sampled at various time points to quantify the total amount of the released PET monomers. The samples were treated as described above and analyzed by HPLC. All experiments were performed in triplicates. Data are presented as the mean values ± SDs.

The thermal stabilities of ScPETaseWT and ScPETaseA212C/T249C were quantified using the substrate pNPB. The enzymes were incubated in water baths at 40 and 50 °C. Enzymes were sampled at various time points to determine esterase activity using the method described above. All experiments were performed in triplicates. Data are presented as the mean values ± SDs.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PET by the Co-expression system
ce:section.ce:para: pET28a-ScPETase-IsMHETase and pET28a-ScPETase plasmids were transformed into E. coli (DE3) cells. Cell induction was performed the same method as described above. The cell pellets were removed by centrifugation at 4 °C and 5000 × g for 15 min. The bacterial solutions and supernatants were used to degrade the PET samples. The comparison of PET hydrolytic activities was performed using 0.6 mmol/L BHET in 1 mL bacterial solution and supernatant and 10 g/L PET (Cry-PET and gf-PET) in 100 mL bacterial solution and supernatant at 30 °C. The reaction mixtures were sampled at various time points to quantify the total amount of the released PET monomers. The samples were treated as described above and analyzed by HPLC. All experiments were performed in triplicates. Data are presented as the mean values ± SDs.

HPLC analysis was performed on a Shimadzu LC-2010A HT apparatus equipped with a Hypersil ODS2-C18 column (5.0 µm, 4.6 × 250 mm). Mobile phases of 80% A (0.1% formic acid) and 20% B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile) were used at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. The hydrolysis products (TPA, mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET), and BHET) were separated at 40 °C and detected at 241 nm. Amounts of TPA, MHET, and BHET were measured using standard curves prepared from commercial TPA (Macklin Inc., China, Cat. No.: P816020) and BHET (Macklin Inc., China, Cat. No.: H909109), and MHET (Macklin Inc., China, Cat. No. B838622).

The 3D protein structure of IsPETase (PDB: 6QGC) was used as a template to simulate the 3D protein structures of PpPETase, ScPETase, and their mutants using the SWISS-MODEL. All non-protein and hydrogen atoms were removed using VMD 1.9.3, and hydrogen atoms on the protein molecules were re-added. A PDB file of the substrate 4-PET was created using Discovery Studio. Finally, docking simulations of 4-PET with PpPETase, ScPETase, and their mutants were performed using AutoDock Vina 1.1.2. Subsequently, suitable small-molecule conformations and proteins were selected using PyMOL 2.5.0 for further investigation.

The 3D protein structure of PpPETase, ScPETase, and their mutants’ molecules were placed inside the water box 12 Å from the edge. Determination of the size and center coordinates of the protein-solvent system, ion neutralization of the solvent environment, and pretreatment of the bound protein and solvent were then performed. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed using GROMACS 2018.33 software and water molecules were modeled using SPC. MD simulations included equilibration and minimization of solvents, energy minimization of ionized proteins, and energy minimization of the protein–solvent systems under NPT (constant number (N), pressure (P), and temperature (T) were regulated) and NVE (constant number (N), volume (V), and energy (E)) conditions in protein dynamics. All MD simulations were performed at a thermodynamic temperature of 300 K and a pressure of 1 bar. The temperature and pressure were controlled using the V-Resale and C-Resale methods. The temperature and pressure coupling constants were 0.2 and 0.5 ps, respectively. The Verlet LeapFrog algorithm was used to solve Newton’s equations of motion, with the integration step set to 2 fs. The MD simulation time was set to 100 ns, and three independent sample simulations were performed to generate visualizations and graphs using PyMOL 2.5.0 software. The root mean square deviation (RMSD) and root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) were obtained during the MD simulations.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Discovery of PpPETase and ScPETase with high PET hydrolytic activity
ce:section.ce:para:
To identify PET hydrolases, sequence homology analysis was conducted using the NCBI database. Eleven potential PET-degrading enzymes (PDs) from various genera were selected, most of which have no documented PET degradation ability. Phylogenetic trees were constructed for the 11 selected PETase candidates and 14 PET hydrolases (
Fig. 1 a; Supplementary Table S3 ). The 25 enzymes were categorized into two distinct groups based on their temperature preferences. The first group consisted of mesophilic enzymes, including IsPETase, and the second group consisted of thermophilic enzymes, such as TfCut2 and LCC ( Fig. 1 a). Although the genera have diverse origins, their protein sequences exhibit a notable level of similarity and contain conserved regions ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Genetic synthesis was performed on the 11 enzymes selected for characterization. The signal peptide is removed from the enzyme during this process. Subsequently, the hydrolytic activity of the 11 potential PET-degrading enzymes was assessed over a broad temperature range from 30 to 50 °C. This evaluation was conducted as a preliminary screening technique using the model substrate pNPB and small-molecule monomers used in the production of PET and BHET. Among the candidates examined, PD2, PD4, PD5, and PD8 exhibited comparatively diminished or imperceptible levels of PET hydrolytic activity under experimental conditions ( Fig. 1 b). Enzymes PD1 and PD9 exhibited significant hydrolytic activity toward PET, surpassing the activities of the other enzymes at all tested reaction temperatures. In particular, PD9 was able to fully break down BHET within 24 h at 30 °C. Therefore, PD1 (NCBI Reference Sequence: WP_220815207.1, PETase derived from P. paralcaligenes MRCP1333, PpPETase) and PD9 (NCBI Reference Sequence: QDI72884.1, PETase derived from S. calvus DSM 41452, ScPETase) were the best PET hydrolases from the pool of 11 PETase hydrolases that were evaluated.

Subsequently, the hydrolytic activities of PpPETase and ScPETase were compared with those of the established PET hydrolases IsPETase and LCC. This comparison encompassed a wide temperature range from 30 and 50 °C, using Cry-PET and gf-PET as substrates. At 30 °C, the hydrolytic activity of PpPETase and ScPETase toward Cry-PET was 1.53- and 3.62-fold higher than that of LCC ( Fig. 1 c), respectively. Furthermore, when Cry-PET was used as the substrate, ScPETase and IsPETase showed comparable degradation efficacies ( Fig. 1 c). Notably, IsPETase has been recognized for its superior hydrolytic activity toward PET at room temperature, surpassing other PET hydrolases documented in the literature [16]. The hydrolytic activity of ScPETase toward Cry-PET at 50 °C was significantly reduced to only 53% of that at 30 °C ( Fig. 1 c). In contrast, the degradation activity of PpPETase toward Cry-PET at 50 °C was 44.28% higher than that at 30 °C ( Fig. 1 c). These differences in degradation activity can be attributed to the significantly higher thermostability of PpPETase compared to ScPETase ( Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3 ). For gf-PET, which has a significantly smaller substrate contact surface area, each enzyme exhibited similar changes, with both newly discovered enzymes performing less well than LCC and IsPETase at 50 °C ( Fig. 1 c). The findings of the present study suggest that both ScPETase and PpPETase have considerable potential as hydrolytic enzymes for PET breakdown, demonstrating their robust PET degradation ability. Nevertheless, it is necessary to increase the thermal stability of ScPETase and PpPETase must undergo rational protein engineering to enhance its degradation activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Structural features and rational protein engineering of PpPETase and ScPETase
ce:section.ce:para:
Pairwise superposition of PpPETase with four different PET hydrolases, IsPETase, RgPETase, LCC, and TfCut2, resulted in global root mean square deviations (RMSD) values of 0.519, 0.583, 0.786, and 0.568 Å, respectively. The presence of two conserved disulfide linkages (C208/C245 and C279/C296) and an extended loop (S248–E253) in the substrate-binding region of PpPETase ( Supplementary Fig. S6 ) indicated that this enzyme likely evolved from a common ancestor shared with IsPETase instead of with LCC or TfCut2 ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ). In the extended-loop structure of PpPETase, Y250 exhibited dissimilarity to N244 in IsPETase ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ). This disparity hinders the ability of the long-chain structure of PET to bind inside the I-shaped groove, leading to decreased efficacy of PpPETase in degrading PET (
Fig. 2 a). This barrier to substrate binding was abolished in the PpPETaseY250N mutant. Compared with PpPETaseWT, PpPETaseY250N exhibited a 2.1-fold increase in the degradation of long-chain PET ( Fig. 2 b). However, there was minimal alteration in the degradation activity of the small-molecule substrate (BHET). The PpPETaseY250N mutation is located in the extended loop, far from the active site, and therefore does not play a direct role in the decomposition of small-molecule substrates. However, the extended loop can be used to stabilize the long-chain structure of PET and thus improve the degradation efficiency [18], as observed for PpPETaseY250N. The MD simulations also indicated that PpPETaseY250N resulted in enhanced the mobility of the extended loop, which helped accommodate the long-chain structure ( Fig. 2 c).

To further enhance the degradation activity of PpPETase, 4-PET was docked into the wide-type PpPETase (
Fig. 3 a), and combinatorial mutations were performed on amino acid residues in the 6 Å range around the substrate binding pocket. In the first round of mutagenesis, single point mutations Y239R, Y239A, A288E, F244A, and F244G significantly enhanced BHET degradation ( Fig. 3 b). Thus, these mutations were combined randomly and eight variants with improved activity were identified. Among these variants, PpPETaseY239R/F244G was the best mutant with a 4.6-fold improvement in degradation activity ( Fig. 3 b); therefore, it was selected as the parent for further engineering. The key site Y250 mentioned above was subjected to saturation mutagenesis and combined with PpPETaseY239R/F244G, and it was found that the mutation of Y250 did not improve the degradation activity against BHET ( Fig. 3 b). However, in the Cry-PET degradation experiments, the concentration of degraded products generated by PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G was enhanced 3.1-fold ( Fig. 3 c). Through molecular docking, it was found that PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G widened the substrate-binding channel of subsite II and facilitated easier binding of long-chain PET to the activity pocket of the enzyme ( Fig. 3 a). MD simulations revealed that the RMSD of PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G was lower than that of the wild-type enzyme, indicating that the overall structure of the substrate-enzyme complex was more stable after engineering ( Fig. 3 d). The flexibility of amino acids in the region near the mutation sites and the active pocket was also enhanced, which was favorable for improving the catalytic activity ( Fig. 3 e).

The global RMSD values for the sequence-independent pairwise superposition of ScPETase with four other PET hydrolases, IsPETase, RgPETase, LCC, and TfCut2 were 0.646, 0.681, 0.594, and 0.515 Å, respectively. The presence of a single conserved disulfide bond (C280/C296) and absence of an extended loop in the substrate-binding region of ScPETase ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ) indicated that this enzyme likely evolved from a common ancestor shared by TfCut2 and LCC, instead of IsPETase ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ). The presence of an additional disulfide bond, as observed in IsPETase, plays a crucial role in differentiating between type I and type II PETase-like enzymes [18]. The second disulfide bond in IsPETase is important for its enzymatic function because it is located close to the active region of the enzyme [18]. To examine the influence of disulfide bonds on the thermal stability and enzymatic activity of ScPETase, a mutant of ScPETase was generated with additional disulfide bonds (
Fig. 4 a). The results indicated that the ScPETaseA212C/T249C mutant exhibited a 1.3-fold increase in half-life at 40 °C and a 2.0-fold increase at 50 °C ( Fig. 4 b). The RMSD value was smaller and more stable for ScPETaseA212C/T249C than ScPETaseWT ( Fig. 4 e), suggesting that these two amino acid conversions effectively increased the overall stability of the ScPETaseA212C/T249C structure in the solvent system. These findings indicated that the introduction of an extra disulfide bond enhanced the thermal stability of ScPETase. Furthermore, the A212C/T249C mutation resulted in an increase in the hydrolytic activity toward PET at 30 and 50 °C, with increases of over 1.5- and 2.3-fold, respectively, compared with ScPETaseWT ( Figs. 4 c and 4 d).

Then, ScPETaseA212C/T249C was used for further engineering experiments. First, single mutations A135E, N195H, and N243K enhanced the degradation of BHET (
Fig. 5 a). The combination of these mutations generated ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K whose activity against BHET increased by 1.6-fold ( Fig. 5 a). In the Cry-PET degradation experiments, the degradation products obtained by ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K were enhanced 1.9-fold ( Fig. 5 b). The mutation N243K places the positively charged lysine next to the negatively charged D215 residue and establishes an intramolecular salt bridge that has been incorporated into several PET-degrading enzyme variants (LCC, ICCM, and Cut190) [26]. The mutation N195H contributed to the formation of a novel hydrogen-bonding network. MD simulations indicated that the stability of the substrate-bound ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K was enhanced compared with that of the wild-type enzyme ( Fig. 5 c), and the flexibility of amino acids adjacent to the mutation sites was improved ( Fig. 5 d).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Co-expression of ScPETase and IsMHETase to degrade PET
ce:section.ce:para:
ScPETase has high efficacy in degrading PET. However, similar to other enzymes that degrade PET, the majority of the degradation by-products (> 90%) consist of MHET with a small amount of TPA [16,36,38,41,43]. Previous research has demonstrated that IsMHETase can facilitate further degradation of MHET into TPA and EG [16,17]. ScPETase can break down BHET rapidly, but most of the material remains as an intermediate product, and MHET and ScPETase cannot completely break down BHET into TPA (
Fig. 6 b). In contrast, IsMHETase displayed comparatively limited degradation activity. The use of the two enzymes in a 1:1 ratio resulted in robust degradation, with TPA as the main degradation product ( Fig. 6 b). However, purification and preparation procedures for ScPETase and IsMHETase are expensive and time-consuming. In terms of industrial application, whole-cell co-expression catalysis has been shown to be a more convenient and practical approach than enzyme purification. Both ScPETase and PpPETase, when equipped with their native signal peptides, both ScPETase and PpPETase are secreted and produced in E. coli. In the culture medium, both enzymes exhibited favorable PET degradation activity. However, the degradation ability of ScPETase was superior to that of PpPETase ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Therefore, IsMHETase, which can effectively degrade MHET, was co-expressed in a secretory expression strain of ScPETase ( Fig. 6 a).

The results demonstrated that both the bacterial solution and supernatant from the strain that only secreted ScPETase were capable of degrading BHET. However, less than 14% of the product was TPA ( Fig. 6 c). In contrast, when the bacterial solution from the co-expressing strain was used, complete breakdown of BHET was possible, resulting in more than 85% TPA. However, similar to the single enzyme, the supernatant from this strain was unable to degrade BHET into its final product ( Fig. 6 c). These results demonstrate that the engineered co-expression system effectively produced two enzymes individually and released ScPETase into the extracellular environment. The scale-up experiments were conducted in shaking flasks. In these experiments, 10 g/L Cry-PET and gf-PET were added to the cultures of both single-enzyme and co-expression strains. Fresh media were provided, and samples were collected every 3 d. The use of the co-expression system resulted in 1.4-fold more degradation than the single enzyme system. After 30 d, the co-expression system degraded Cry-PET and gf-PET by more than 40% and 6%, respectively ( Fig. 6 d). The percentages of TPA in the Cry-PET and gf-PET degradation products were 37.7% and 25.6%, respectively ( Fig. 6 d). These results demonstrate the efficacy of the co-expression system in breaking down long-chain PET, a molecule that is too large to enter cells. PET degradation is achieved by the secretion of ScPETase into the extracellular space, where it converted into smaller molecules. These smaller molecules are further broken down by IsMHETase, producing the final TPA product. Thus, complete degradation of PET was successfully achieved.

Because of the growing concern regarding plastic waste as an environmental problem, an increasing amount of research has focused on enzymatic PET depolymerization as a sustainable solution for the treatment and reuse of plastic waste. Extensive research has been conducted to identify and characterize the PET-degrading enzymes. To date, approximately 30 such enzymes have been identified and studied in detail [44–46]. In the present study, two PET-degrading enzymes (PpPETase and ScPETase) were identified. These enzymes are derived from distinct genera and exhibit degradation activities at room temperature. This suggests that PET-degrading enzymes are widely prevalent in natural environments. The co-expression method developed in the present study enabled the continuous breakdown of PET at room temperature and required less time and financial expenditure than the traditional method of bacterial culture followed by protein purification. The developed system has significant potential for industrial applications.

Metagenomics technology has been extensively used to search for plastic-degrading enzymes, and we successfully identified two novel PET-degrading enzymes using this technique. The first plastic-degrading enzyme to be discovered, IsPETase, was discovered by screening colonies that had been exposed to PET in the environment for an extended period [16]. However, this research method yields only a limited number of cultivable microorganisms and requires complex and time-consuming experiments. In contrast, metagenomic technology can be used to streamline the screening processes. The present study demonstrates the efficacy of the metagenomic method as a robust tool for identifying and evaluating new, highly targeted enzymes with specialized activities. In the future, a more comprehensive investigation of the human and environmental microbiomes will enable further identification of strains and proteins that can degrade PET and other types of plastics.

The PpPETase enzyme was derived from P. paralcaligenes MRCP1333. To the best of our knowledge, this particular strain was obtained from human feces [47], making it the first documented instance of a PET hydrolase present in human gut bacteria. Microplastics are found in the human gastrointestinal tract [10]. Humans have the potential to mechanically digest plastics, leading to the generation of microplastics. Previous research has indicated that microplastics have the potential to affect the human digestive system and modify the composition of the gut microbiota [48]. This finding, together with the discovery of the PET hydrolase MG8 in the human salivary metagenome [49], suggests that contamination caused by microplastics may affect the human body, and humans may be developing microorganisms that can metabolize microplastics. The results of the present study provide further evidence of the link between microplastics and intestinal infections in humans. Furthermore, this study highlights the need for increased awareness of the potential effects of microplastics on human health.

The Streptomyces strains to which ScPETase belongs have received less attention in research on the breakdown of synthetic polymers than in studies on bioremediation [50]. Although Streptomyces has been well-studied for its ability to produce bioactive compounds, our understanding of the potential of Streptomyces enzymes to degrade esters is limited. To the best of our knowledge, ScPETase is the first documented PET-degrading enzyme to be isolated from Streptomyces. The degradation activity of ScPETase is commendable and justifies further investigation and potential enhancement of the enzyme to improve its degradation ability. Type Ⅰ enzymes, predominantly present in thermophilic actinomycetes, function at optimal temperatures of > 60 °C [31,33]. In contrast, ScPETase is better suited for reactions conducted at ambient temperatures. Thus, ScPETase provides a novel platform for the efficient decomposition of PET at ambient temperatures.

In summary, PpPETase and ScPETase were identified through gene mining in two different bacteria. These two enzymes can degrade semicrystalline PET powder and low-crystallinity PET films at room temperature. Through structure-guided engineering, two variants, PpPETaseY239R/F244G/Y250G and ScPETaseA212C/T249C/N195H/N243K were obtained that decompose Cry-PET 3.1- and 1.9-fold faster than their wild-type enzymes, respectively. Furthermore, a ScPETase-IsMHETase co-expression system was developed, which showed a faster degradation process and higher TPA concentration in the degradation of PET powder and film than a single-enzyme system. The discovery of these two novel PET hydrolases provides opportunities to create more powerful biocatalysts for PET biodegradation.
